share_verdict: Half pulse, half grain. Now it is rice with a rumour of dal.

source.text: Kṛsara is described across the Sanskrit culinary and medical literature, including the Mānasollāsa
source.century: Pre-12th CE, with the Mānasollāsa description 12th CE

ingredients.name: mung dal, split
ingredients.function: the protein half of the dish, and the reason kṛsara is prescribed to the convalescent — mudga is the pulse the medical texts treat as lightest

ingredients.name: hand-pounded rice
ingredients.function: the starch half. Hand-pounding leaves most of the bran on, so it cooks slower and holds together

ingredients.name: sesame
ingredients.quantity_modern: 2 tbsp, or sesame oil for the tempering
ingredients.function: the fat, and a substantial part of the calcium and iron. Tila is what kṛsara is named around in several descriptions

ingredients.name: ginger
ingredients.function: digestive; standard with heavy pulse dishes

method_reconstructed: Dry-roast the mung dal in an earthen pot until it smells nutty.
Wash the rice; combine dal and rice roughly one to one.
Boil with several times the volume of water until both collapse into each other.
Temper sesame, ginger and cracked pepper in sesame oil or ghee and stir through.
contested_points: Kṛsara is described in more than one text and the proportions differ between them; the one-to-one ratio here is a reasonable middle, not a quoted figure.
Whether sesame or the pulse is the defining ingredient depends on which description you follow.

changed.from: roughly equal parts pulse and rice
changed.to: rice-dominant, with a token quantity of dal
changed.driver: pulse acreage fell as land moved toward export and cash crops, and pulses became the expensive ingredient on the plate rather than the cheap one
mechanised rice milling stripped bran and germ at scale, and polished rice stored and shipped better

changed.from: sesame or another regional cold-pressed fat
changed.driver: industrial solvent extraction and refining made a cheap, neutral, long-shelf-life oil available everywhere

ingredients: 1 cup hand-pounded or single-polished rice (any kirana that sells 'hand pounded' or red rice)
steps: Dry-roast the dal in the pot until it smells nutty. This is the step people skip and it is the one that makes the difference.
Add rinsed rice and five cups of water. Simmer covered 25 minutes until it is soft enough to eat with a spoon and not a fork.
Heat the sesame oil, crackle the sesame seeds, add ginger and pepper, pour it in.
A cold-pressed fat with a real flavour is doing work here — the tempering is most of the taste. This is where a named oil matters.

verification.note: Seed record. Kṛsara appears in several texts and the composite description here has not been checked against any single printed edition, so no verse number or page is claimed.
